subject: Edge networking plan & tradeoffs for Private deployment (VPC peering / PrivateLink / S2S VPN)
body:
--- Original message 1/4 ---
From: Alex Romero <alex@medicax.com>
To: Camila Reyes <camila_reyes@redwood.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 18 Feb 2026 09:12:00 -0800
Subject: Private deployment network options (MedicaX)

Hi Camila / Lauren,

Thanks again for the chat this morning. MedicaX is moving fast — we need a secure, non‑internet path for PHI traffic between our VPCs and Redwood Private. The security team has an initial blocker: no egress through the public internet for inference requests or logging.

Can you lay out the practical differences and tradeoffs between:
- VPC Peering (cross-account peering)
- AWS PrivateLink / endpoint services
- Site‑to‑Site VPN (on‑prem termination)

Key constraints:
- HIPAA environment (no internet egress for PHI)
- Multi‑account setup (MedicaX infra in 3 AWS accounts across prod/staging/logging)
- Low single-digit 10s ms latency for inference is preferred
- Want minimal ops burden on our infra team

If you could include which approach Redwoods recommends for a Private deployment and any configuration gotchas (CIDR overlap, route propagation, MTU, NAT) that would be great. Also any docs or short checklist we can pass to our network team.

Regards,
Alex
Director, IT Infrastructure — MedicaX

--- Reply 2/4 ---
From: Camila Reyes <camila_reyes@redwood.com>
To: Alex Romero <alex@medicax.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 18 Feb 2026 11:03:00 -08:00
Subject: Re: Private deployment network options (MedicaX)

Alex — thanks for the clear list. I put together a concise pros/cons + practical checklist below and attached our one‑pager (redwood_vpc_connectivity_cheatsheet.pdf) for the network team.

Short summary / recommendation (tl;dr):
- If MedicaX cannot allow any PHI to traverse the public internet, PrivateLink is usually the cleanest from a security posture: it keeps traffic inside AWS’s private network and avoids cross-account route table propagation.
- If you need the absolute lowest latency and full L3 network access (e.g., host‑level debug, custom protocols), VPC Peering gives simpler hop behavior but requires strict CIDR planning and cross‑account route management.
- Site‑to‑Site VPN is appropriate when you need to connect on‑prem gear to Redwood Private or as a temporary fallback, but it has variable latency and management overhead.

Detailed tradeoffs (bullet format for easy pass‑through):
1) AWS PrivateLink (Endpoint Service)
   - Pros:
     • No public IPs: traffic stays on Amazon backbone, supports strict egress controls.
     • Simple from customer side: create an interface endpoint in each consumer VPC and allow principal access.
     • Works across accounts/regions (with endpoint in each region).
     • Better security posture for regulated data (supports HIPAA workflows).
   - Cons / gotchas:
     • Interface endpoints (ENIs) consume IPs — plan CIDR carefully.
     • Does not provide full L3 reachability (only the service ports you expose).
     • Cross‑region: you need endpoints per-region and accompanying config.
     • Costs: hourly ENI endpoint + data processing charge (usually less than egress NAT/GW at scale but depends on traffic).

2) VPC Peering (Cross‑account)
   - Pros:
     • Native L3 route visibility, minimal additional hops (low latency).
     • No intermediate proxies — good for stateful debugging and non‑HTTP protocols.
   - Cons / gotchas: 
     • CIDR non‑overlap required; cross‑account route table maintenance can be error prone at scale.
     • Peering is regional (unless using Transit Gateway). Multi‑account, multi‑region is complex.
     • Does not support transitive routing — you'd need Transit Gateway for hub‑and‑spoke.
     • Security: higher blast radius if route tables are misconfigured.

3) Site‑to‑Site VPN
   - Pros:
     • When connecting on‑prem gear (air‑gapped or legacy), VPN is the natural choice.
     • Can be used as encrypted fallback/resiliency path between sites.
   - Cons / gotchas: 
     • Latency jitter and throughput limits depending on provider; not ideal for strict P95 latency.
     • MTU and fragmentation issues (common with path MTU discovery) — recommend 1400 MTU baseline tests.
     • Operational burden: key rotation, monitoring, and furtive rekeys.

When to combine approaches:
- PrivateLink + S2S VPN: use PrivateLink for service traffic (no Internet egress) and S2S to support on‑prem tools or admin pipelines.
- Transit Gateway: If MedicaX wants hub‑and‑spoke across many accounts and regions, set up a Transit Gateway with attachments for each account and use either PrivateLink or TGW attachments for Redwood.

Quick config checklist for your network team (high level):
- Confirm CIDR ranges for all consumer VPCs — ensure no overlaps with Redwood infra ranges.
- Decide per‑region endpoints or peering; map a table: Account -> VPC -> Region -> Option chosen.
- If PrivateLink: reserve /24 per endpoint subnet (infra dependent), add least‑privileged policy to the endpoint service, and test ENI IP consumption.
- If Peering: prepare route‑propagation runbook and automation scripts for creating cross‑account peering and route table updates.
- If S2S VPN: standardize on ikev2, confirm MTU, BGP vs static routing decision, and define RTO for rekeys.

Next steps I propose:
1) Karthik — can you add any Redwood runtime constraints (KV cache behavior, connection pooling per ENI, HTTP keepalive limits) that would push MedicaX toward one option?
2) Alex — confirm whether you can create interface endpoints in each VPC (cost/ops) or whether MedicaX prefers a peering model.
3) I’ll put a short SOW stub and a timeline estimate after we pick an option.

Thanks,
Camila Reyes
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

Attachment: redwood_vpc_connectivity_cheatsheet.pdf

--- Internal note / Reply 3/4 ---
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
To: Camila Reyes <camila_reyes@redwood.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 19 Feb 2026 10:22:00 -08:00
Subject: Re: Private deployment network options (MedicaX)

Quick tech addendum (keeping it short):

- Runtime connections: our Private deployment accepts inbound TLS (mutual TLS optional) over specific ports. We prefer long‑lived HTTP/2 or persistent HTTP/1.1 keepalives to avoid repeated TLS handshakes — that interacts with clients behind interface endpoints/ENIs the same as plain VPC networking.
- ENI density: for PrivateLink, each interface endpoint creates ENIs in selected subnets. If MedicaX has many small subnets, they can exhaust IPs — recommend at least /24 available in each AZ where you plan endpoints.
- KV cache locality: to preserve low latency we try to keep inference workers in the same AZ as the incoming traffic; cross‑AZ hops add ~2–3 ms typically, cross‑region adds 40–100+ ms. Peering offers the fewest hops inside the region.
- Port & protocol needs: PrivateLink will only expose the service ports we choose to publish. If you need non‑HTTP ports for observability tooling, peering or TGW is needed.
- Monitoring expectations: handshake/drop patterns behind PrivateLink can look like green/close cycles for TCP; ensure VPC flow logs and ENI metrics are enabled to correlate.

Practical recommendation for MedicaX (given HIPAA/no internet egress constraint):
1) Primary: PrivateLink in each prod VPC (keeps PHI on AWS backbone, limited blast radius, straightforward access control).
2) For on‑prem admin tooling and any host‑level access: establish a Site‑to‑Site VPN from on‑prem to a MedicaX transit VPC and use bastion/CICD jumpboxes — do not route PHI over the VPN unless you have the same policy constraints and encryption audits.
3) If MedicaX expects to scale to dozens of VPCs, use a Transit Gateway for routing and consider an endpoint service fronted by TGW to reduce per‑VPC ENI sprawl.

I’ve attached a quick checklist/commands we hand to customers during onboarding in the cheatsheet.

—Karthik
Principal Software Engineer (Inference) | Redwood Inference

--- Final message 4/4 ---
From: Alex Romero <alex@medicax.com>
To: Camila Reyes <camila_reyes@redwood.com>
Cc: MedicaX IT Ops <itops@medicax.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>
Date: Fri, 20 Feb 2026 15:27:00 -08:00
Subject: Re: Private deployment network options (MedicaX)

Camila / Karthik — thanks, that is very helpful and exactly what we needed. Quick decisions from our side after an internal security review: 

- We will proceed with PrivateLink as the primary connectivity method for prod (HIPAA requirement: no public internet egress for PHI).
- We will create interface endpoints in each of our three prod VPCs (one per region where applicable).
- We will also set up a Site‑to‑Site VPN into our transit VPC for ops/admin traffic and for on‑prem CI runners — we will not route inference PHI over the VPN.

Action items:
- MedicaX (IT): create a short table of VPC IDs, subnets per AZ (preferred endpoint AZs), and confirm available CIDR space (before Tuesday 24 Feb). Attachment: medicax_security_questionnaire_v2.xlsx filled by our infra team.
- Redwood (Camila / Karthik): draft SOW + timeline and include estimated endpoint costs and configuration runbook. Also please include testing plan for MTU and low‑latency verification.

We are aiming for a pilot in the week of Mar 9 (internal change freeze permitting). Please include the cost estimate in the SOW so procurement can queue the purchase order.

Alex
Director, IT Infrastructure — MedicaX
